items.title: Inverse-problem models and solution classes

references.title: Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, Chapter 3, printed pp. 15–27
Tristan van Leeuwen and Christoph Brune, 10 Lectures on Inverse Problems and Imaging, Lecture 1 §§1.2–1.3

items.statement:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

items.title: Identifiability and stability moduli

references.title: Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.2 and Chapter 4 §4.1
Tristan van Leeuwen and Christoph Brune, 10 Lectures on Inverse Problems and Imaging, Lecture 1 §§1.2–1.3

items.statement:
Use metric spaces $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$, a nonempty admissible truth class $U\subseteq X$, a forward map $F:U\to Y$, and a metric solution-class space $(Q,d_Q)$ with class map $q:U\to Q$ as follows: $q$ has image all of $Q$, and $q(x)=q(x')$ exactly when $x$ and $x'$ are equivalent for recovery. The library's metric axioms imply nonnegative metric values.

The forward map $F$ is **identifiable modulo the recovery equivalence on $U$** if

$$x,x'\in U\text{ and }F(x)=F(x')\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q(x)=q(x').$$

It is nonidentifiable modulo that equivalence if some two admissible truths have equal data and distinct target classes.

A **deterministic data-only estimator** is a function $\widehat q:Y\to Q$. It is exact on $U$ if $\widehat q(F(x))=q(x)$ for every $x\in U$. The diagram below commutes exactly under this condition; it states the defining equality of functions and is not a proof device.

```tikzcd
U \arrow[r,"F"] \arrow[dr,"q"'] & Y \arrow[d,"\widehat q"] \\
& Q
```

A **uniform stability modulus on $U$** is a nondecreasing function $\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, with $\omega(0)=0$ and $\lim_{t\downarrow0}\omega(t)=0$, such that

$$d_Q(q(x),q(x'))\le\omega\bigl(d_Y(F(x),F(x'))\bigr)\qquad(x,x'\in U).$$

Identifiability concerns equality of exact data; the modulus is a separate quantitative bound for all truth pairs. The estimator definition specifies no regularization procedure or convergence guarantee.

items.title: Kernel directions preclude unrestricted recovery

references.title: Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 §4.1
Tristan van Leeuwen and Christoph Brune, 10 Lectures on Inverse Problems and Imaging, Lecture 1 §§1.2–1.3

items.statement:
Let $(X,d_X)$, $(Y,d_Y)$, and $(Q,d_Q)$ be metric spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth class, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, and let $q:U\to Q$ assign each truth its target class. Let $x_0,x_1\in U$, let $\delta\ge0$, and suppose a single datum $y\in Y$ satisfies

$$d_Y(y,F(x_0))\le\delta\quad\text{and}\quad d_Y(y,F(x_1))\le\delta.$$

For every deterministic data-only estimator, meaning every function $\widehat q:Y\to Q$, the two target-class losses at that datum satisfy

$$\max\{d_Q(\widehat q(y),q(x_0)),d_Q(\widehat q(y),q(x_1))\}\ge\frac12d_Q(q(x_0),q(x_1)).$$

In particular, if $F(x_0)=F(x_1)$ but $q(x_0)\ne q(x_1)$, no data-only estimator exactly recovers both truths. The quantitative bound also holds whenever the radius-$\delta$ data balls around the two forward data share the observed datum $y$.

title: Inverse maps, identifiability, and stability — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Kernel ambiguity, an unstable diagonal inverse, and a constrained class

references.title: Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.2 and Chapter 4 §4.1
Tristan van Leeuwen and Christoph Brune, 10 Lectures on Inverse Problems and Imaging, Lecture 1 §§1.2–1.3
Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems, §1.2 (scope context)

items.statement:
For $n=1,2$, give $\mathbb R^n$ the metric $d_1(x,z)=\sum_{k<n}|x_k-z_k|$, using the coordinatewise real vector-space structure. In the first model take parameter space and admissible truth class $X=U=\mathbb R^2$, data space $Y=\mathbb R^1$, and identity recovery target $Q=U$ with $q=\operatorname{id}_U$ and the restricted $d_1$ metric. Define $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^1$ by $A(a,b)=(a)$, take $F:=A$, and define $\ker A:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:A(x)=(0)\}$. Then $\ker A=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$ is nontrivial. The truths $x_0=(0,0)$ and $x_1=(0,1)$ have the same exact datum $(0)$ and target-class distance $d_1(x_0,x_1)=1$, so every deterministic data-only estimator at that datum has worst-case loss at least $1/2$.

Let $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and use the real Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, let $e_n$ be the sequence with value $1$ at $n$ and $0$ elsewhere. Define the diagonal map $D:\ell^2\to\ell^2$ by $(Dx)_n=(1/2)^n x_n$. In the second model take $X=U=Y=Q=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical norm metric $d_2(x,z)=\|x-z\|_2$, forward map $F:=D$, and identity target map $q=\operatorname{id}_U$. This map is well-defined, linear, and injective, hence identifiable, but it has no uniform stability modulus on all of $\ell^2$: $\|e_n\|_2=1$ and $\|De_n\|_2=(1/2)^n\to0$. For each $n$, the observed datum $y=0$ lies within noise radius $\delta=(1/2)^n$ of both $D(0)$ and $D(e_n)$, so every deterministic data-only estimator at $y=0$ has worst-case loss at least $1/2$.

Finally, restrict $A$ to $U_0:=\{(a,0):a\in\mathbb R\}$ and use $U_0$ itself as the target class with its inherited $d_1$ metric. The restricted map is identifiable, and its inverse $\widehat q((a))=(a,0)$ is an isometry; the function $\omega(t)=t$ is a uniform stability modulus. This restriction removes the particular kernel ambiguity above.
